title: The tank method
subtitle: Fresh and fruity bubbles
objectives: Explain how the tank method works
Explain why it suits aromatic grapes
Compare it with the traditional method

steps.title: How it works
steps.body: In the tank method, also called Charmat or Martinotti, the base wine goes into a sealed, pressurised tank with sugar and yeast. The second fermentation takes days or weeks. The wine is then filtered under pressure and bottled. The whole process can take as little as a month.
steps.highlight: Second fermentation in a pressurised tank

steps.title: Why aromatic grapes suit it
steps.body: Glera, Muscat and similar grapes have delicate floral and fruit aromas. Long contact with yeast would cover them with bready notes. The tank method keeps them fresh. It is also cheaper and faster, so the wines are affordable, made to drink young, and usually show larger, softer bubbles than Champagne.
steps.highlight: Tank: fresh fruit, made to drink young

steps.prompt: Which wine is typically made by the tank method?
steps.explanation: Prosecco is made by the tank method. Champagne, Cava and Franciacorta use the traditional method.

steps.body: Keep tank-method wines in a cool place and drink them within a year or two. Their charm is freshness, and it doesn't last.

steps.prompt: What are typical features of tank-method sparkling wine?
steps.explanation: Bread and biscuit notes come from long ageing on lees in bottle, typical of the traditional method.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The tank method ferments in sealed tanks, often in weeks
It preserves fresh fruit and floral aromas
It's faster and cheaper, and the wines are best young
